Pregnancy

Dizziness and feeling faint during pregnancy

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy can make you feel light-headed, particularly when standing up quickly, becoming overheated or going too long without food or fluids. These episodes can have several causes. Being common does not mean that every episode should be dismissed as a routine part of pregnancy.

First, protect yourself from a fall

If you feel faint, stop what you are doing and sit down promptly. If the feeling does not pass, lie on your side and ask someone to stay nearby. Do not try to walk it off, climb stairs or drive while dizzy.

In later pregnancy, lying flat on your back can make faintness worse because the uterus may press on major blood vessels. Turn onto your side if symptoms occur in that position. If you lose consciousness, the person helping should seek emergency assistance if you do not recover promptly or have other serious symptoms.

Consider everyday triggers without diagnosing yourself

Hormonal changes can lower blood pressure, and standing still for a long time can allow blood to collect in the legs. Heat, dehydration and missed meals may also contribute. Low iron levels or other medical conditions can be relevant, especially when symptoms recur.

Dizziness is not proof of low blood sugar, and the baby is not simply taking blood away from your brain. Note what you were doing, how long the episode lasted and whether you had other symptoms. This can help the maternity team decide what to assess.

Sweating, weakness and hunger can accompany low blood glucose, but those symptoms also occur for other reasons. Pregnancy hormones relax blood vessels, so blood pressure may fall even while total blood volume is increasing. Later, pressure from the growing uterus can reduce blood returning to the heart when you lie flat.

Loosen tight or heavy clothing and move to a cooler, well-ventilated place when it is safe to do so. If you are about to faint, first sit or lie down; wait until you are alert and the dizziness has eased before having water or a snack.

Make small changes that reduce avoidable triggers

Rise slowly from bed or a chair, allowing a moment to sit before standing. Avoid prolonged standing where possible and move away from an overly hot or stuffy environment. Take care getting out of a warm bath or shower.

Drink regularly and avoid skipping meals. Smaller, more frequent amounts may be easier when nausea makes eating difficult. If vomiting prevents you from keeping fluids down, contact your maternity team; repeated dehydration needs more than simply trying another snack.

Know when to get help urgently

Seek urgent medical assessment for dizziness that is severe, persistent or repeatedly returning, and after a first fainting episode. Tell the clinician that you are pregnant. A fall involving the head or abdomen also needs prompt advice, as does a change in your baby’s usual movements.

Get emergency help for dizziness or faintness with chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, major visual changes, severe abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. In early pregnancy, pain with faintness can be a sign of an ectopic pregnancy. Do not wait to see whether food or rest resolves a concerning combination of symptoms.

Review recurring symptoms with your maternity team

Even if each episode settles, repeated faintness deserves a conversation. The team may review blood pressure, hydration, blood count, medicines and other possible contributors. What is checked depends on the pattern and your medical history.

If you have diabetes, follow your agreed plan for suspected low blood glucose and tell the team about repeated episodes. Do not adjust medicines or start high-dose iron solely because you feel dizzy. A clear explanation and individualized plan are more useful than assuming that increasing pregnancy weight must make dizziness progressively worse.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

HSE advises slow position changes, regular food and fluids, avoiding overheating and side-lying when faint.

Recurrent dizziness needs assessment; a first faint, injury or associated pain, bleeding, chest symptoms or severe headache needs urgent advice.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to prepare a short account of the position, meals, heat exposure and other symptoms around each episode for your maternity visit.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for faintness with severe abdominal pain, bleeding, chest pain, breathlessness or severe headache, or if a person does not recover promptly after fainting.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Sit down promptly and lie on your side if faintness persists.
  • Hydration, regular meals and slower position changes may help with common triggers.
  • Fainting, persistent symptoms or warning signs require medical assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Does dizziness always mean low blood sugar?

No. Blood-pressure changes, dehydration, anemia and other causes may be involved.

Should I ignore dizziness because it is common in pregnancy?

No. Recurrent or severe symptoms, fainting or accompanying warning signs should be assessed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
